gloss: gerah, one twentieth of a shekel, throat or neck, stir up strife
summary: The census contribution, valuations and redemption payments all use a shekel of twenty gerahs. Ezekiel specifies the same ratio when calling for honest measures. The noun גָּרוֹן denotes the neck that bears a necklace and the throat from which a voice comes. The verb describes provoking a quarrel or joining battle. In Psalm 39 the sufferer calls the blow of God’s hand an assault.

words.gloss: gerah, one twentieth of a shekel

senses.gloss: gerah, one twentieth of a shekel
senses.definition: A small unit of weight. Twenty make one shekel by the standard given in the biblical passages.

evidence.note: The census offering is half a sanctuary shekel, and the full shekel is defined as twenty gerahs.
The standard applies to the sanctuary valuations.
The payment for each firstborn beyond the number of Levites is five shekels at twenty gerahs to the shekel.
The same reckoning applies to redemption from a month old.
The prophet specifies twenty gerahs to the shekel alongside the reckoning of the mina.

senses.definition: Calling out leaves the psalmist’s throat parched. Isaiah tells the prophet to cry out at full voice. Psalm 5 compares the throat of those who speak deceitfully to an open grave.
Isaiah depicts the women of Zion walking with outstretched necks. In Ezekiel a chain is placed around the neck.
An angry person stirs up strife between others.
Israel is forbidden to contend with Edom, and later summoned to engage Sihon in battle.
The speaker asks God to remove a plague, saying the assault of his hand has spent him. This is the noun’s only occurrence.

evidence.locator: G, pp. 96–97, girû A, BE 8 3:15 and YOS 6 112

cognates.gloss: front or underside of the neck

note: The Akkadian unit is usually reckoned at one twenty-fourth of a shekel. CAD also discusses a possible twelfth in one account. The biblical texts consistently specify a twentieth. The identical Hebrew spelling in the dietary laws means ‘cud’. The index groups the throat under גרה. Arabic jirān supports the meaning of the body part. Its connection to the Hebrew unit of weight remains uncertain. The relationship between inciting strife and the nouns for weight and throat remains unclear.
